Infectious mononucleosis: 4

A patient with EBV mononucleosis develops a diffuse rash after amoxicillin. There was no immediate wheezing or circulatory collapse. Which interpretation avoids automatically applying a permanent IgE-mediated allergy label without appropriate subsequent assessment?

  1. Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis
  2. Reactive cytotoxic T lymphocytes
  3. Early negative heterophile testing does not exclude EBV
  4. Splenic rupture risk
  5. An aminopenicillin-associated rash during EBV infection
Answer and explanation

An aminopenicillin-associated rash during EBV infection

A rash after amoxicillin in EBV does not automatically establish permanent IgE-mediated penicillin allergy.

Option explanations

An aminopenicillin-associated rash during EBV infection: A rash after amoxicillin in EBV does not automatically establish permanent IgE-mediated penicillin allergy.

Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis: Fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and atypical lymphocytes are a classic presentation. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Reactive cytotoxic T lymphocytes: The atypical lymphocytes in EBV mononucleosis are largely activated T cells responding to infected B cells. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Early negative heterophile testing does not exclude EBV: Test sensitivity depends on timing and age; EBV-specific serology may be appropriate when suspicion persists. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Splenic rupture risk: Splenic enlargement during mononucleosis makes contact sports or abdominal trauma hazardous until medically cleared. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
